It is that noise produced by the multitude of distant noise sources which together make up the background noise level sometimes referred to as the "urban roar". The key feature of residual noise is that it is a direct measure of the sound produced by the urbanization process.
The measurement survey revealed that:
 Residual noise levels vary from 41 to 53 dBA in the daytime and 36 to 49 dBA in the nighttime, which correspond to Ldn noise levels between 46-69.
 Most areas of the City, except near the airport and on heavily traveled streets and highways experience noise levels that are below Ldn 76.
 A significant number of public and semi-public sites in central San Jose experience higher-than-average noise levels.
 A significant amount of the area adjacent to the heavily traveled streets experience noise levels greater than Ldn 60.
A summary of noise levels for various areas of the City is given in Table V and representative residual and mode levels are given as standard noise levels in dBA. Also given is the day to night change in residual and mode level and the Ldn value. The Ldn value is a day-night equivalent noise level which considers noise exposure over a 24-hour period and weighs noise events as a function of time period.
More detail noise level information is available from a series of twenty noise contour maps at a 1 inch = 2,000 feet scale, which cover the entire area of the City. Each map contains shaded areas indicating the approximate zone where a certain level of sound may be found. These zonal (noise

) areas will increase or decrease depending on weather conditions, time of day, and volume of traffic. The maps indicate the existing (1974) and projected (1995) noise zones throughout the San Jose Sphere of Influence. The 1995 noise contours indicate those areas where the noise zones will have some change due to alterations in surface traffic volumne the addition of new rights-of-way, or new technology in equipment design.
Contours are provided for Ldn levels of 60 to 70, 70 to 80, and over 80, reflecting the standards set by City policy on noise levels. These contour maps are available for reference at the San Jose City Planning Department. The present general noise factor in each of the CDBG neighborhoods is examined below, from the General Plan Noise Element.
Alma CNRA:
The Alma neighborhood is entirely within the Ldn 60-70 contours, with Ldn 70-80 contours along Alma Avenue and Monterey Highway, extending westerly of the latter approximately 100 feet. The 1995 projections do not indicate any reduction in the current noise levels, nor any additions which would affect this area.
